reading.exampleNote: The small reader-guide table contains invented interactions.

title: Matching a Reader’s Interests to Guide Descriptions
blurb: Guide descriptions give us evidence even before a guide has been opened. Represent topics explicitly and compare them with a reader’s interests.
openingTitle: Can a New Guide Be Useful Before Anyone Has Read It?
opening: A new guide about soil moisture has no opens, so popularity puts it last. Yet it might be exactly what a reader asking about irrigation needs.
We can compare what the guide covers with what the reader wants. First we need matching topic coordinates, then a similarity rule whose treatment of length we understand.

history.title: Using the Description of an Item

sources.title: Salton, Wong and Yang: A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing (1975)

blocks: Vector-space information retrieval represented documents using shared term coordinates, allowing a query and a document to be compared numerically. This provides a foundation for using item descriptions in retrieval and recommendation.

Our guides use two hand-labelled topic coordinates so the comparison is inspectable. Real systems may use terms or learned embeddings, but the coordinate meaning and similarity assumptions still matter.

quiz.prompt: What is cosine similarity?
quiz.because: Length is divided out.

given.data: Reader [1,0], guide [3,0].

quiz.prompt: Its cosine direction is well defined.
quiz.because: Its norm is zero.

given.data: An item vector is [0,0].

quiz.prompt: What must be fixed first?
quiz.because: Positions must represent the same features.

given.data: One vector orders features [water,light], another [light,water].

quiz.prompt: Content similarity can score it without previous clicks.
quiz.because: It uses descriptions rather than interaction counts.

given.data: A newly published guide has a usable topic vector.

build.title: Match topic directions
build.problem: Botie has one reader profile and one candidate guide.
build.challenge: Take their dot product and divide by the product of their lengths.
build.why: Normalising removes length so direction drives this comparison.
build.limitation: Requires nonzero vectors with matching feature meanings. A score is not a calibrated probability.

intuition.title: Use the same coordinates
intuition.explanation: Both vectors order topics as irrigation then lighting.

intuition.title: Remove length when it is irrelevant
intuition.explanation: Cosine compares direction by normalising both vector lengths.

intuition.title: Compare topic direction
intuition.explanation: The irrigation guide points along the reader’s interest.

parts.title: 1. Make Coordinates Comparable
paragraphs: An item vector and reader vector must use the same feature order and preparation. A value for irrigation cannot be compared with a value for lighting just because they occupy the same position in differently constructed arrays.
A profile may come from an explicit request or an average of previously liked item vectors. That averaging is a modelling choice: a reader may have several distinct interests that one average hides.
interpretation: Start with labelled topic features before introducing opaque learned coordinates.

parts.title: 2. Choose Whether Magnitude Should Matter
paragraphs: A dot product rewards alignment and length. Cosine divides by both vector norms so multiplying one vector by a positive constant leaves the score unchanged.
This is helpful if magnitude reflects document length rather than relevance. It is less appropriate if magnitude intentionally expresses confidence or strength that the task needs to retain.
parts.calculation:
Cosine(a,b) = dot(a,b) / (norm(a) × norm(b))
Reader = [1,0]; guide = [3,0]
Cosine = 3 / (1 × 3) = 1
interpretation: A zero vector has no direction; define a fallback instead of dividing by zero.

parts.title: 3. Score Before Selecting
paragraphs: For a catalogue matrix with one guide per row, normalise each row and multiply by a normalised reader vector. The output has one score per guide. Sort those scores only after availability and exclusion rules are clear.
A high similarity is a model score, not a probability that the reader will enjoy the guide. Its numerical scale depends on the representation.
interpretation: The NumPy example exposes row norms rather than hiding normalisation inside a recommendation call.

examples.title: A longer description need not be a different direction
paragraphs: The reader and guide use the same two content features. Compare the guide with a version whose coordinates are both ten times larger.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
reader = np.array([1., 1.])
guide = np.array([2., 2.])
for description in [guide, 10 * guide]:
    similarity = (reader @ description) / (np.linalg.norm(reader) * np.linalg.norm(description))
    print(f'{similarity:.3f}')
interpretation: Both descriptions point in the reader's direction, so scaling alone does not improve the cosine match. Practice compares several genuinely different directions.

parts.title: 4. Check What the Description Leaves Out
paragraphs: Content-based ranking can recommend a new item from its features, but cannot use a feature that was never recorded. It may also repeatedly suggest near-duplicates and fail to introduce a reader to useful unfamiliar subjects.
Evaluate on later interactions and inspect diversity and coverage alongside relevance. Cold-start readers still need an initial request or another fallback.
interpretation: The workshop compares two nonzero vectors. The next lesson uses patterns shared across readers.

practice.title: Can you score the guide descriptions?
practice.question: Can you score the guide descriptions?
task: Compute cosine scores for each nonzero guide row and the reader. Print scores rounded to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
items = np.array([[3.,0.],[0.,2.],[1.,1.]])
reader = np.array([1.,0.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
items = np.array([[3.,0.],[0.,2.],[1.,1.]])
reader = np.array([1.,0.])
unit_items = items/np.linalg.norm(items,axis=1,keepdims=True)
unit_reader = reader/np.linalg.norm(reader)
print(np.round(unit_items @ unit_reader,3).tolist())
hints: Keep the row dimension when dividing by norms.
The output has one value per item.

practice.title: Does a longer description change its direction?
practice.question: Does a longer description change its direction?
task: Calculate cosine for both rows against the reader and print to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
items = np.array([[1.,2.],[10.,20.]])
reader = np.array([2.,1.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
items = np.array([[1.,2.],[10.,20.]])
reader = np.array([2.,1.])
scores = items @ reader / (np.linalg.norm(items,axis=1)*np.linalg.norm(reader))
print(np.round(scores,3).tolist())
hints: Both rows have the same direction.
The positive scale cancels in numerator and denominator.

reading.experimentTitle: Does the guide describe what this reader is interested in?
reading.experimentIntro: Compare the profile and guide by direction. Scale a description without changing its proportions and check whether that alone makes the guide a better match.
reading.connectionTitle: A shared feature description makes an interest comparison possible
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Rank Descriptions Against a Reader Profile
reading.outputLabel: Cosine similarity between reader and guide
reading.exampleNote: The profile and description coordinates are supplied illustrative features.

title: Learning From Readers With Similar Preferences
blurb: A guide’s description may miss what readers value. Shared ratings let Botie compare preferences, provided missing ratings remain distinct from dislikes.
openingTitle: What Did Readers With Similar Tastes Find Useful?
opening: Two readers agree on several guides, even though those guides cover different subjects. Their shared preferences may reveal something that topic labels missed.

Collaborative filtering uses patterns across readers and items. We will start with an explicit rating table and a weighted neighbour prediction, keeping each reader’s usual rating level separate from their deviations.

history.title: Sharing Judgements Across Readers

sources.title: GroupLens: An Open Architecture for Collaborative Filtering of Netnews (1994)

blocks: GroupLens explored collaborative filtering for netnews, using readers’ ratings to help predict which articles others would find interesting. Shared judgements supplied information that the article text alone might not capture.
Our small rating table uses the same broad idea, but the workshop is a transparent neighbourhood calculation rather than a recreation of the original service.

quiz.prompt: What deviations should be combined?
quiz.because: Subtract each neighbour’s own mean.

given.data: Ratings [5,3], neighbour means [3,4].

quiz.prompt: It can safely be included as an explicit negative rating.
quiz.because: Missing does not mean disliked.

given.data: A missing rating is stored as zero without a mask.

quiz.prompt: What should the prediction procedure do?
quiz.because: There is no weighted evidence.

given.data: All selected neighbour weights sum to zero.

quiz.prompt: Their reliability deserves scrutiny.
quiz.because: Agreement with little overlap is weak evidence.

given.data: Similarities are based on just one common rating.

build.title: Predict a reader’s rating
build.problem: Botie has positive neighbour similarities and their observed ratings for the candidate.
build.challenge: Subtract neighbour means, compute a weighted average of deviations, then add the target reader’s mean.
build.why: Centred deviations preserve preference relative to each neighbour’s rating scale.
build.limitation: Weights must be non-negative with positive total. Missing neighbours are excluded before this calculation.

intuition.title: Separate taste from rating scale
intuition.explanation: Some readers give higher ratings generally.

intuition.title: Compare deviations
intuition.explanation: A rating above a neighbour’s own mean indicates unusual enthusiasm.

intuition.title: Adjust the target reader’s baseline
intuition.explanation: Transfer the weighted deviation, not the neighbours’ raw rating scale.

parts.title: 1. Keep Missing Ratings Missing
paragraphs: Store an observed mask alongside the rating values, or use a missing marker deliberately. A missing rating is not a zero-star review. Means, overlap counts, and similarities must use only observed entries.
Two readers who share only one rated item provide fragile similarity evidence. Require enough overlap or shrink unreliable similarities rather than treating every apparent agreement equally.
interpretation: Training means must be computed from training ratings only.

parts.title: 2. Compare Preferences After Centering
paragraphs: Subtract each reader’s observed-rating mean from their ratings. This separates a tendency to rate everything highly from a preference for one item relative to that reader’s usual level.
A neighbourhood model estimates similarity on co-rated items. Here those similarities are supplied so we can examine the prediction step. Positive weights only are used in this teaching example.
interpretation: A supplied similarity is an input to this exercise, not a claim that similarity estimation is solved.

parts.title: 3. Transfer a Weighted Deviation
paragraphs: For neighbours who rated the candidate, calculate their deviations from their means. Weight and average those deviations, then add the target reader’s mean.
parts.calculation:
Neighbour deviations = [5-3, 3-4] = [2,-1]
Weighted deviation = (0.75 × 2 + 0.25 × -1) / 1 = 1.25
Prediction = 3 + 1.25 = 4.25
interpretation: If no suitable neighbours rated the item, use an explicit baseline rather than divide by zero.

examples.title: Interpret one neighbour relative to their usual rating
paragraphs: This neighbour usually rates guides at two but gave this guide four. The target reader's own average is three.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
neighbour_rating = 4.0
neighbour_mean = 2.0
target_mean = 3.0
deviation = neighbour_rating - neighbour_mean
print(deviation)
print(target_mean + deviation)
interpretation: The transferable evidence is the neighbour's positive deviation from their usual rating. Practice combines several such deviations with different similarity weights.

parts.title: 4. Evaluate Sparse and New Cases
paragraphs: Collaborative filtering needs shared interaction evidence. New readers, new items, and readers with unusual tastes may have little overlap. Compare these groups separately instead of relying only on an overall score.
Rating prediction error does not directly measure whether the top few recommendations are useful. We will distinguish those evaluation questions after learning a compact model of the rating table.
interpretation: The workshop returns a raw rating estimate; clipping to a rating range is a separate declared choice.

practice.title: Can you predict from centred neighbour ratings?
practice.question: Can you predict from centred neighbour ratings?
task: Print the target reader’s estimated rating to two decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
ratings = np.array([5.,3.])
means = np.array([3.,4.])
weights = np.array([.75,.25])
target_mean = 3.
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
ratings = np.array([5.,3.])
means = np.array([3.,4.])
weights = np.array([.75,.25])
target_mean = 3.
prediction = target_mean + weights @ (ratings-means)/weights.sum()
print(f'{prediction:.2f}')
hints: Calculate deviations before weighting.
Add the target reader’s baseline last.

practice.title: Can you compute means without treating missing as dislike?
practice.question: Can you compute means without treating missing as dislike?
task: Use NaN as missing. Print each reader’s observed count and mean rounded to two decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
rating = np.array([[5.,np.nan,3.],[np.nan,2.,4.]])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
rating = np.array([[5.,np.nan,3.],[np.nan,2.,4.]])
observed = ~np.isnan(rating)
print(observed.sum(axis=1).tolist())
print(np.round(np.nanmean(rating,axis=1),2).tolist())
hints: Count the mask, not nonzero ratings.
These rows each contain at least one observed value.

reading.experimentTitle: What does a neighbour's rating mean on their own scale?
reading.experimentIntro: A generous reader and a strict reader can both like the same guide. Change their typical ratings and compare the centred preferences before weighting them by similarity.
reading.connectionTitle: Neighbour preferences are more useful when their baselines are visible
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Predict Ratings Without Treating Missing as Dislike
reading.outputLabel: Rating predicted from centred neighbour preferences
reading.exampleNote: Neighbour similarities and observed ratings are supplied teaching values.

title: Compressing a Sparse Table of Preferences
blurb: A rating table can be enormous and mostly empty. Small vectors for readers and guides can share information across its observed entries.
openingTitle: Do We Need a Separate Rule for Every Reader and Guide?
opening: Botie’s rating table grows whenever a reader joins or a guide appears. Most reader-guide pairs have no rating, so storing a learned prediction independently for every pair would miss the shared structure.
Matrix factorisation gives each reader and item a short learned vector. Their dot product predicts a rating, and observed ratings teach both sets of vectors.

history.title: Sharing Information Through Latent Factors

sources.title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky: Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems (2009)

blocks: Koren, Bell and Volinsky described matrix-factorisation methods that became prominent in recommender systems, including work associated with the Netflix Prize. Learned low-dimensional factors allowed user and item information to interact.
The coordinates are learned to fit the objective. They should not automatically be labelled with human interests such as humour or difficulty unless additional evidence supports that interpretation.

quiz.prompt: What is their predicted rating?
quiz.because: Multiply and sum matching coordinates.

given.data: Reader [1,2], item [2,1].

quiz.prompt: Squared-error training should always treat it as zero.
quiz.because: Use the observed mask.

given.data: An unobserved cell has no rating.

quiz.prompt: Which reader vector belongs in the item gradient?
quiz.because: Both gradients are evaluated at one parameter state.

given.data: Both factor vectors are updated simultaneously.

quiz.prompt: Its human meaning is not uniquely determined by the ratings.
quiz.because: Equivalent factorisations can make the same predictions.

given.data: A factor coordinate changes under a rotation that preserves dot products.

build.title: Score all candidate guides
build.problem: Botie has a reader factor vector and one factor row per guide.
build.challenge: Multiply the guide matrix by the reader vector to obtain one score per guide.
build.why: A shared coordinate system lets one reader vector score every candidate row.
build.limitation: Factors must already be fitted from training observations. Scores are not probabilities.

intuition.title: Give each side a short vector
intuition.explanation: Coordinates must align between reader and item factors.

intuition.title: Predict by combining coordinates
intuition.explanation: The dot product gives one pair’s score.

intuition.title: Update only from an observed rating
intuition.explanation: The prediction error moves both vectors.

parts.title: 1. Define the Two Factor Matrices
paragraphs: Store one vector per reader in U and one per guide in V. Their matrix product with V transposed gives a full score table. Factor width is a modelling choice that controls capacity.
A rating model often also includes a global mean and reader/item biases. We omit those here to isolate the factor interaction, not because offsets are unimportant.
interpretation: Latent coordinates can rotate without changing predictions, so they do not have unique meanings.

parts.title: 2. Fit Observed Entries Only
paragraphs: Use a mask to identify training ratings. A squared-error objective sums errors on those entries; unobserved cells are not zero-rating targets. Regularisation can discourage excessively large factors.
Implicit feedback requires a different interpretation of observations and often a different objective or confidence scheme. Do not silently reuse an explicit-rating loss on clicks.
parts.calculation:
Prediction = dot([1,2], [2,1]) = 4
Observed rating = 5
Residual = 4 - 5 = -1
interpretation: The residual is defined as prediction minus observation throughout this lesson.

parts.title: 3. Update Both Vectors From the Same Old State
paragraphs: For half squared error on one pair, the reader gradient is residual times the old item vector, and the item gradient is residual times the old reader vector. Make copies before updating either in place.

If the second update uses the already-changed first vector, it implements a different step from the simultaneous gradient calculation. Add regularisation gradients consistently if the objective includes them.
interpretation: The coding exercise deliberately saves both old vectors so the dependency is visible.

examples.title: Find both gradients before changing either factor
paragraphs: One observed rating is four, while the supplied reader and guide factors predict a smaller value. Calculate each gradient from the original pair.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
reader = np.array([1., 0.])
guide = np.array([2., 1.])
rating = 4.0
error = reader @ guide - rating
print(float(error))
print((error * guide).tolist())
print((error * reader).tolist())
interpretation: Each factor's gradient uses the other factor as it was before the update. Practice turns those gradients into two parameter updates without letting the first change contaminate the second.

parts.title: 4. Check More Than Training Reconstruction
paragraphs: Low training error can reflect memorisation, especially with many factors and few ratings. Tune factor width and regularisation against held-out ratings or ranking tasks. Split by time when predicting future behaviour.
A brand-new item has no fitted factor. A content-based model or fallback is still needed. Learned factors do not solve missing exposure or biased feedback by themselves.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop computes a score from supplied factors; fitting is shown in Python.

practice.title: Can you update a pair of factors correctly?
practice.question: Can you update a pair of factors correctly?
task: Use half squared error without regularisation and rate 0.1. Print both updated vectors rounded to two decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
u = np.array([1.,2.])
v = np.array([2.,1.])
rating, rate = 5., .1
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
u = np.array([1.,2.])
v = np.array([2.,1.])
rating, rate = 5., .1
old_u, old_v = u.copy(), v.copy()
error = old_u @ old_v-rating
u -= rate*error*old_v
v -= rate*error*old_u
print(np.round(u,2).tolist())
print(np.round(v,2).tolist())
hints: Compute the residual from old vectors.
Copy arrays before changing them in place.

practice.title: Can you ignore the unobserved cells?
practice.question: Can you ignore the unobserved cells?
task: Calculate mean squared error only where observed is true. Print it to two decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
predicted = np.array([[4.,3.],[2.,5.]])
rating = np.array([[5.,0.],[0.,3.]])
observed = np.array([[True,False],[False,True]])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
predicted = np.array([[4.,3.],[2.,5.]])
rating = np.array([[5.,0.],[0.,3.]])
observed = np.array([[True,False],[False,True]])
error = predicted[observed]-rating[observed]
print(f'{np.mean(error**2):.2f}')
hints: Select by the mask before calculating a mean.
The zeros are storage placeholders.

reading.experimentTitle: How does one reader vector score several guides?
reading.experimentIntro: The reader and guide factors use the same coordinates. Change one factor and follow which candidate scores increase, decrease or remain unchanged.
reading.connectionTitle: Shared factors can describe preferences without filling every missing rating
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Update Factors Using Observed Ratings
reading.outputLabel: Predicted scores in guide order
reading.exampleNote: The factors are supplied for inspection; missing ratings are not observed zeros.

title: Checking the List a Reader Actually Sees
blurb: A recommender usually shows a short list. Evaluate that list’s relevant items, their positions, and the cases where little history is available.
openingTitle: Did the Useful Guide Reach the First Few Results?
opening: Botie may rank a useful guide correctly relative to most of the catalogue and still place it below everything the reader sees. Average rating error does not directly answer whether the visible list helped.
We will evaluate a fixed candidate set at a chosen cutoff, then distinguish finding relevant guides from putting the most useful ones near the top.

history.title: Evaluating the Recommendation Task

sources.title: Herlocker and colleagues: Evaluating Collaborative Filtering Recommender Systems (2004)

blocks: Herlocker and colleagues emphasised that evaluating a recommender involves the user task, data, metrics, and experimental design. A numerical comparison is meaningful only when these choices match the intended use.
Our exercise fixes the candidate set, relevance labels, and list length. That lets us calculate exactly what a metric rewards before drawing conclusions about a live recommendation system.

quiz.prompt: What is recall at three?
quiz.because: Two of four relevant items were retrieved.

given.data: Top-three binary relevance [1,0,1], four relevant candidates overall.

quiz.prompt: Their ranking scores are automatically directly comparable.
quiz.because: Candidate difficulty changes the task.

given.data: Two systems use different sampled candidate sets.

quiz.prompt: What does the implementation need?
quiz.because: There is no positive ideal gain to normalise.

given.data: Ideal DCG is zero.

quiz.prompt: It can still fail on users with no interaction history.
quiz.because: Cold starts require separate evidence.

given.data: A system scores existing users well.

build.title: Measure usefulness in the visible list
build.problem: Botie has binary relevance labels for the guides actually shown.
build.challenge: Add relevant hits and divide by the number shown.
build.why: The denominator matches the number of recommendations the reader received.
build.limitation: Use a nonempty binary list at a fixed cutoff. This computes precision, not recall or NDCG.

intuition.title: Inspect the visible list
intuition.explanation: Each value indicates whether a ranked guide is relevant.

intuition.title: Count useful results
intuition.explanation: Precision divides by list length; recall divides by all relevant candidates.

intuition.title: Respect the order
intuition.explanation: Discounted gain gives earlier relevant positions more weight.

intuition.title: The first useful result can matter even when precision is unchanged
intuition.explanation: These lists contain the same number of relevant guides. Their precision is equal, but one makes the reader pass an irrelevant result before finding something useful. A position-sensitive measure can capture that difference.

scene.caption: Two illustrative recommendation orders.

parts.title: 1. Fix the Candidate Set and Cutoff
paragraphs: Specify which items could have been recommended at the prediction time. Exclude unavailable items and make the handling of previously seen items explicit. A list evaluated against ten sampled negatives can produce a different score from one ranked against the whole catalogue.
Choose a cutoff that matches what the reader sees. Keep training interactions out of held-out relevance labels.
interpretation: Comparisons need the same candidates and exclusion rules.

parts.title: 2. Separate Precision From Recall
paragraphs: Precision at k is the fraction of the returned k items that are relevant. Recall at k is the fraction of all relevant candidates that appear there. The denominators answer different questions.
When no relevant candidates are labelled for a reader, recall is undefined unless an aggregation convention is declared. Do not silently create a perfect score.
parts.calculation:
Top-three relevance = [1,0,1]; total relevant candidates = 4
Precision@3 = 2/3
Recall@3 = 2/4 = 0.5
interpretation: These metrics ignore ordering within the selected top-k set.

parts.title: 3. Give Earlier Positions More Weight
paragraphs: Discounted cumulative gain divides a gain by a logarithmic rank discount. NDCG normalises by the best possible ordering of the same relevance labels at the same cutoff. Define whether gains are binary, raw graded relevance, or exponential graded gains.
Our example uses binary gains. If ideal gain is zero, report the declared zero or exclusion convention instead of dividing by zero.
parts.calculation:
Binary DCG = sum(relevance_at_rank / log2(rank + 1))
Ranks start at 1
NDCG = observed DCG / ideal DCG
interpretation: A perfect ordering gives one when positive ideal gain exists.

examples.title: Count relevance at the part of the list being shown
paragraphs: There are three relevant guides in the catalogue. Only the first two recommendations are visible in this comparison, and one of those is relevant.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
relevance = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])
visible = relevance[:2]
total_relevant = 3
print(f'{visible.mean():.3f}')
print(f'{visible.sum() / total_relevant:.3f}')
interpretation: Half of the visible list is useful, but it retrieves only one third of the relevant catalogue. The denominators answer different questions.

parts.title: 4. Inspect New Readers and New Guides Separately
paragraphs: Average per-reader metrics so highly active readers do not dominate unintentionally. Report performance for sparse histories and cold starts, along with catalogue coverage and repeated recommendations.

Offline labels reflect past exposure and may miss items a reader would have liked. A live experiment can assess actual behaviour, but it needs an explicit objective and careful interpretation rather than treating clicks as the whole goal.
interpretation: The workshop calculates precision from a supplied visible list. Python also checks position-sensitive gain.

practice.title: Can you distinguish precision from recall?
practice.question: Can you distinguish precision from recall?
task: Print precision and recall at three to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
relevant = np.array([1,0,1])
total_relevant = 4
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
relevant = np.array([1,0,1])
total_relevant = 4
print(f'{relevant.mean():.3f}')
print(f'{relevant.sum()/total_relevant:.3f}')
hints: Use list length for precision.
Use total relevant candidates for recall.

practice.title: How much does placing the relevant guide second cost?
practice.question: How much does placing the relevant guide second cost?
task: Use binary gains and cutoff two. Print DCG, ideal DCG and NDCG to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
relevance = np.array([0.,1.])
discount = np.log2(np.arange(1,3)+1)
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
relevance = np.array([0.,1.])
discount = np.log2(np.arange(1,3)+1)
dcg = np.sum(relevance/discount)
ideal = np.sum(np.sort(relevance)[::-1]/discount)
print(f'{dcg:.3f}')
print(f'{ideal:.3f}')
print(f'{dcg/ideal:.3f}')
hints: Rank one has a discount denominator of one.
Sort relevance descending for the ideal ordering.

reading.experimentTitle: How useful was the list the reader actually saw?
reading.experimentIntro: Keep the displayed list separate from the full catalogue. Change which shown guides are relevant and compare the useful count with the number of recommendations delivered.
reading.connectionTitle: Ranking quality is judged at the list the reader receives
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Compare Relevant Items and Their Positions
reading.outputLabel: Precision of the displayed list
reading.exampleNote: The relevance labels are invented judgements for the displayed guides.

title: Finding Unusual Readings Without Letting Them Set the Reference
blurb: A faulty sensor can pull an ordinary mean toward itself. Use a robust centre and spread, then decide what a large deviation actually warrants.
openingTitle: Should a Broken Sensor Help Define What Looks Normal?
opening: Most of Botie’s pressure readings are close together, but one is much larger. If that reading helps determine the average and spread used to judge it, it can make itself look less unusual.
A median centre and median absolute deviation give us a reference less sensitive to extreme values. They identify unusual observations under a reference distribution, not the cause of a fault.

history.title: Estimating a Reference Despite Contamination

sources.title: Huber: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter (1964)

blocks: Huber’s work formalised robust estimation under departures from an assumed model. The practical concern is that a few contaminated observations should not determine an entire estimate.
Our median and median-absolute-deviation score is a simple robust teaching example, not Huber’s specific estimator. It lets us inspect how the reference changes when an extreme reading is present.

quiz.prompt: What is its median?
quiz.because: The middle ordered value is ten.

quiz.prompt: This proves the instrument is faulty.
quiz.because: A genuine unusual event can also score highly.

given.data: A reading has a high anomaly score.

quiz.prompt: What is the raw MAD score?
quiz.because: Use absolute distance divided by MAD.

given.data: Median=10, raw MAD=1, new reading=13.

quiz.prompt: The implementation needs an explicit handling policy.
quiz.because: The raw division is undefined.

given.data: MAD equals zero.

build.title: Score new pressure readings
build.problem: Botie has reference records and separate incoming readings.
build.challenge: Find the reference median, calculate its MAD, then divide incoming absolute deviations by that spread.
build.why: The reference is fitted separately and the spread resists a small number of extreme values.
build.limitation: Requires positive MAD. A large score indicates unusualness, not a diagnosed fault.

intuition.title: Find a typical centre
intuition.explanation: A median uses order rather than the size of an extreme tail.

intuition.title: Measure typical distance from it
intuition.explanation: Take absolute deviations and their median.

intuition.title: Score a new reading
intuition.explanation: Compare its distance with that fixed reference spread.

parts.title: 1. Define the Reference Population
paragraphs: Choose records that represent the operating condition in which the detector will be used. A pressure normal during startup may be unusual during steady operation. Split reference fitting from later threshold selection and final testing.
An anomaly score measures disagreement with the reference. It does not tell us whether an observation is a sensor fault, a genuine event, or a new operating regime.
interpretation: The same numerical deviation can have different meanings in different conditions.

parts.title: 2. Calculate Centre and Spread Separately
paragraphs: The median is a central ordered value. The median absolute deviation, or MAD, is the median of distances from that centre. Neither step requires squaring a large deviation.
parts.calculation:
Reference = [8,9,10,11,100]
Median = 10
Absolute deviations = [2,1,0,1,90]
MAD = 1
interpretation: The centre and spread should be retained for scoring later records.

parts.title: 3. Make the Score’s Convention Explicit
paragraphs: Our raw score divides absolute distance from the median by MAD. A commonly used normal-consistency scaling multiplies MAD by approximately 1.4826; that produces a different numerical score and threshold.

We use the raw convention throughout this lesson. If MAD is zero, many reference values coincide. Do not silently divide by zero or insert an unexplained epsilon: define a fallback scale, exact-match policy, or a different model.
parts.calculation: Raw score for 13 = abs(13-10) / 1 = 3
interpretation: A threshold has meaning only together with the score definition and reference data.

examples.title: Measure spread around the middle reading
paragraphs: Begin with an orderly reference sample. Find its middle value, measure every absolute departure from it, then take the middle departure.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([4., 5., 6., 7., 8.])
centre = np.median(reference)
departures = np.abs(reference - centre)
print(float(centre))
print(departures.tolist())
print(float(np.median(departures)))
interpretation: The MAD is one in the original measurement units. Practice adds an extreme reference value and then scores a separate incoming reading.

parts.title: 4. Turn a Score Into a Reviewed Alert
paragraphs: Select a threshold using representative validation records and the cost of missed faults versus unnecessary investigations. Evaluate precision and recall when reliable labels exist, and inspect the burden of alerts per day.
Updating the reference automatically with every incoming reading can gradually absorb a developing fault. Decide which records are eligible to update the baseline and keep versions for comparison.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop fits a median reference, then scores separate new readings.

practice.title: Can you fit a robust reference?
practice.question: Can you fit a robust reference?

title: Judging a Reading Against Its Neighbours
blurb: Different operating regimes can have different spreads. Local outlier factor compares a point’s density with the density around its neighbours.
openingTitle: Can a Sparse Group Be Normal?
opening: One pump runs under tightly controlled pressure, while another normally varies more. A single global distance threshold can flag the second pump’s ordinary readings and miss a gap inside the first pump’s tight group.
A local comparison asks whether a point is much more isolated than the points around it. We will build that comparison from neighbours, reachability distances, and local densities.

history.title: Outliers Relative to Their Surroundings

sources.title: Breunig, Kriegel, Ng and Sander: LOF (2000)

blocks: The LOF paper introduced a degree of outlierness based on local density rather than a single global distance threshold. Its comparison lets regions with different densities provide their own local reference.

Our one-dimensional example avoids distance ties to expose the mechanism. The original neighbourhood definition includes ties at the kth-neighbour distance, which can make a neighbourhood contain more than k points.

quiz.prompt: What is the mean density ratio?
quiz.because: Divide each neighbour density by the point density before averaging.

given.data: Point density=0.5; neighbour densities=[1,2].

quiz.prompt: The point’s local density is roughly similar to its neighbours’ densities.
quiz.because: That is what the ratio compares.

given.data: LOF is close to one.

quiz.prompt: What is reachability(p,o)?
quiz.because: Use the larger value.

given.data: Distance(p,o)=2 and kth_distance(o)=5.

quiz.prompt: Local density comparison is guaranteed to detect every member.
quiz.because: Members can look typical relative to each other.

given.data: An anomaly group is internally dense.

build.title: Compare a point with its local surroundings
build.problem: Botie has reachability distances and the neighbours’ own densities.
build.challenge: Average reachability, take its reciprocal, divide neighbour densities by that density, then average the ratios.
build.why: The score compares density at the point with density nearby.
build.limitation: Inputs must come from the same neighbourhood rule. This stage does not construct neighbour sets.

intuition.title: Find neighbours excluding the point itself
intuition.explanation: For k=1, each point uses its nearest other point.

intuition.title: Calculate local reachability density
intuition.explanation: Use the larger of actual distance and the neighbour’s own kth distance.

intuition.title: Compare with neighbour density
intuition.explanation: A much lower density than neighbours gives a larger ratio.

parts.title: 1. Choose a Distance and Neighbourhood
paragraphs: Scale features using a training reference so units do not dominate distance. For each point, find its kth-neighbour distance after excluding itself. Include all neighbours within that distance when implementing the original tie convention.
The neighbourhood size sets the scale of comparison. Too small a neighbourhood can be unstable; too large one can mix different operating regimes.
interpretation: The exercises use distinct nearest-neighbour distances to avoid an ambiguous tie rule.

parts.title: 2. Prevent Tiny Distances From Dominating
paragraphs: The reachability distance from a point to a neighbour is the maximum of their distance and the neighbour’s kth-distance. Notice whose kth-distance is used: the neighbour’s.

This lower bound prevents an extremely close pair from producing arbitrarily large local density just because their mutual distance is tiny. It does not guarantee a positive denominator when duplicates dominate.
parts.calculation:
reachability(p,o) = max(distance(p,o), kth_distance(o))
local_density(p) = 1 / mean(reachability(p, neighbours))
interpretation: Duplicate-only neighbourhoods need a declared numerical policy.

parts.title: 3. Compare Density Ratios
paragraphs: For each neighbour, divide its local density by the point’s density, then average. A value near one indicates density similar to the neighbourhood. A substantially larger value indicates the point is sparser than its neighbours.
parts.calculation:
Point 10 has local density 1/9
Its nearest neighbour at 1 has density 1
LOF = 1 / (1/9) = 9
interpretation: LOF is not an anomaly probability, and one is not a universal hard decision threshold.

examples.title: Compare one local density with its neighbours
paragraphs: Suppose the reachability distances for this point are both two. Its two neighbours have the supplied local densities. The question is how their average density compares with this point's density.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
reachability = np.array([2., 2.])
neighbour_density = np.array([0.5, 1.0])
own_density = 1.0 / reachability.mean()
print(float(own_density))
print(float(np.mean(neighbour_density / own_density)))
interpretation: The neighbours are denser on average. Practice starts earlier in the procedure, calculating neighbours and reachability from the point coordinates.

parts.title: 4. Separate Fitting From Scoring New Points
paragraphs: The classic training-set calculation includes each reference point’s neighbourhood. Scoring a new observation against a fixed reference is a related novelty-detection procedure and must avoid silently rebuilding the reference with the new point.
Inspect sensitivity to k, distance scaling, and contamination. The method can miss a group of anomalies that forms a dense group of its own.
interpretation: The workshop combines supplied reachability distances and neighbour densities. The Python example computes them from raw points.

practice.title: Can you calculate LOF for three points?
practice.question: Can you calculate LOF for three points?
task: Use k=1 with no distance ties. Print local densities rounded to three decimals and LOF values to one decimal.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0.,1.,10.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0.,1.,10.])
distance = np.abs(x[:,None]-x[None,:])
np.fill_diagonal(distance,np.inf)
nearest = np.argmin(distance,axis=1)
kdist = distance[np.arange(len(x)),nearest]
reach = np.maximum(kdist,kdist[nearest])
density = 1/reach
lof = density[nearest]/density
print(np.round(density,3).tolist())
print(np.round(lof,1).tolist())
hints: Exclude each point’s diagonal before finding neighbours.
Reachability uses the selected neighbour’s kth distance.

practice.title: Can you compare several neighbour densities?
practice.question: Can you compare several neighbour densities?
task: Use the supplied reachability distances to compute the point’s density and its LOF. Print both to two decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
reachability = np.array([2.,4.])
neighbour_density = np.array([.5,1.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
reachability = np.array([2.,4.])
neighbour_density = np.array([.5,1.])
density = 1/reachability.mean()
score = np.mean(neighbour_density/density)
print(f'{density:.2f}')
print(f'{score:.2f}')
hints: Density is reciprocal mean reachability.
Average neighbour-to-point density ratios.

title: Finding Readings That Are Easy to Separate
blurb: An isolated reading often needs few random splits to stand apart. Follow paths through small trees before averaging that evidence across a forest.
openingTitle: How Many Splits Does It Take to Isolate One Reading?
opening: Four pressure readings sit close together and another lies far away. A split placed somewhere across their range often separates the distant reading immediately, while the close readings need more splits.
Isolation forests use this difference in path length. They repeatedly partition samples at random and score observations by how quickly they become isolated.

history.title: Detecting by Isolation Rather Than Density

sources.title: Liu, Ting and Zhou: Isolation Forest

blocks: Liu, Ting and Zhou developed isolation-based anomaly detection, using random partitions to separate observations. The method estimates how easily a point can be isolated without first fitting a full density.

Our first tree has supplied splits so every branch can be followed. The second exercise averages path lengths from several trees. A production forest fits many random trees on subsamples and handles depth limits and unresolved leaves.

quiz.prompt: What is its edge-count path length?
quiz.because: It passes one split.

given.data: One record is isolated by the root split.

quiz.prompt: The conventional isolation score increases.
quiz.because: The score decreases with path length.

given.data: Mean path length decreases while subsample size stays fixed.

quiz.prompt: Which size determines c(n)?
quiz.because: Normalise by the training subsample size.

given.data: There are 100 trees, each trained on 256 records.

quiz.prompt: It is a calibrated probability that a sensor is broken.
quiz.because: Isolation measures unusual separability.

given.data: A high isolation score is observed.

build.title: Score isolation paths
build.problem: Botie has this reading’s path length in each tree and the positive sample-size normaliser.
build.challenge: Average paths, divide by the normaliser, negate, then raise two to that exponent.
build.why: Averaging reduces dependence on one partition, and shorter paths receive higher scores.
build.limitation: Paths must come from fitted trees with a consistent subsample size and leaf correction policy.

intuition.title: Start with separated values
intuition.explanation: One value lies beyond a compact group.

intuition.title: Make a first split
intuition.explanation: A threshold at ten isolates the last value.

intuition.title: Continue splitting the compact group
intuition.explanation: The distant point has a shorter path in this example.

parts.title: 1. Build a Random Partition Tree
paragraphs: Choose a feature with variation and a threshold between its minimum and maximum in the current subset. Divide records, then repeat inside each child. Stop when a record is isolated or a declared limit is reached.
A one-dimensional example needs only thresholds. In several dimensions, random feature choices also matter. Store the actual tree: prediction follows its splits rather than drawing fresh thresholds.
interpretation: The hand-chosen tree here illustrates traversal, not random training.

parts.title: 2. Count Edges Along a Path
paragraphs: Path length counts the splits passed before reaching the leaf. A point isolated by the root split has length one. Closely packed observations tend to require more partitions, although any one random tree can be misleading.
parts.calculation:
Root threshold = 10
Left-child threshold = 1.5
Its child thresholds = 0.5 and 2.5
Paths for [0,1,2,3,20] = [3,3,3,3,1]
interpretation: When a depth-limited leaf still contains multiple records, standard scoring adds an expected remaining-path correction.

parts.title: 3. Average Trees and Normalise
paragraphs: Average path lengths across fitted trees. The conventional score uses a normalising expected path length for the training subsample size, then applies a decreasing exponential. Shorter average paths produce larger scores.
The normaliser depends on sample size, not the number of trees. Our exercise uses the harmonic-number expression directly for a small sample.
parts.calculation:
c(n) = 2 H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n, for n > 1
score = 2^(-mean_path / c(n))
interpretation: The score is a relative isolation measure, not a calibrated probability of failure.

examples.title: Combine the path lengths from two trees
paragraphs: One tree isolated the observation after one split; another needed three. Average those path lengths before converting them to a score using the supplied sample-size normaliser.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
paths = np.array([1., 3.])
normaliser = 4.0
mean_path = paths.mean()
score = 2.0 ** (-mean_path / normaliser)
print(float(mean_path))
print(f'{score:.3f}')
interpretation: The average reduces reliance on one lucky partition. Practice asks you to obtain path lengths by actually following a tree's branches.

parts.title: 4. Decide How to Investigate Alerts
paragraphs: Fit on representative records, assess validation alerts, and inspect effects of subsampling and feature representation. An unusual but valid operating mode may also be easy to isolate.

A contamination setting often determines a score cutoff; it does not prove the true fraction of faulty records. Use labelled incidents and operational costs when available, and preserve a route for a person to review the evidence.
interpretation: The workshop aggregates paths. Its numerical tests check the direction of the score as path length changes.

practice.title: Can you follow every split in the tree?
practice.question: Can you follow every split in the tree?
task: Represent an internal node as (threshold,left,right) and a leaf as None. Print path lengths for the supplied readings.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

tree = (10., (1.5, (.5,None,None), (2.5,None,None)), None)
# Write your calculation here.
hints: Each visited internal node contributes one.
Choose left only when the value is strictly below the threshold.

practice.title: Which reading is easiest to isolate across trees?
practice.question: Which reading is easiest to isolate across trees?
task: Each row contains paths from one fitted tree for the same five readings. Calculate conventional scores with subsample size five. Print the index of the highest score and whether all scores lie between zero and one.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
paths = np.array([[3.,3.,3.,3.,1.],[2.,3.,4.,4.,1.]])
n = 5
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
paths = np.array([[3.,3.,3.,3.,1.],[2.,3.,4.,4.,1.]])
n = 5
harmonic = np.sum(1/np.arange(1,n))
normaliser = 2*harmonic-2*(n-1)/n
scores = 2**(-paths.mean(axis=0)/normaliser)
print(int(np.argmax(scores)))
print(bool(np.all((scores>0)&(scores<1))))
hints: Average down tree rows.
A shorter path receives a larger exponential score.

title: Detecting Patterns a Model Cannot Reconstruct
blurb: A model trained to reproduce normal sensor patterns can expose departures through reconstruction error. The error still needs a validated alert rule.
openingTitle: What Does Botie’s Model Fail to Rebuild?
opening: Normal pump operation produces related pressure and flow readings. A reconstruction model learns to reproduce those patterns through a restricted representation.
A new combination may reconstruct poorly, even if neither reading is unusual alone. We will separate the reconstruction, the error score, and the decision to alert.

history.title: Using Reconstruction as Evidence

sources.title: Hinton and Salakhutdinov: Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks (2006)

blocks: Hinton and Salakhutdinov demonstrated learning compact representations with neural networks by reconstructing data. A reconstruction objective teaches what information must survive compression.
Using reconstruction error as an anomaly signal is an additional modelling choice. A network may reconstruct some anomalies well, and a normal condition absent from training may reconstruct poorly.

quiz.prompt: What is mean squared reconstruction error?
quiz.because: Average the two squared coordinate errors.

given.data: Input [1,3], reconstruction [1,1].

quiz.prompt: Reconstruction-based detection can miss it.
quiz.because: The score depends on error, not the hidden cause.

given.data: A model reconstructs one anomaly accurately.

quiz.prompt: Does the rule alert?
quiz.because: The comparison is strict.

given.data: Alert rule is score > 2. The score is exactly 2.

quiz.prompt: Future false-alarm rate is guaranteed to equal five percent.
quiz.because: Future distributions and true labels can differ.

given.data: A threshold is the 95th reference percentile.

build.title: Decide which reconstructed records need review
build.problem: Botie has prepared readings, their reconstructions, and a fixed threshold.
build.challenge: Calculate squared differences, average each row, then compare strictly above the threshold.
build.why: The score aggregates feature mismatch before the threshold turns it into an alert.
build.limitation: Models and preprocessing must already be fitted. Alerts need investigation and are not fault diagnoses.

intuition.title: Prepare comparable features
intuition.explanation: Scores should not be dominated by arbitrary units.

intuition.title: Calculate feature errors
intuition.explanation: Keep both errors visible before reducing.

intuition.title: Apply a declared alert rule
intuition.explanation: Average error and compare with a validation-selected threshold.

parts.title: 1. Fit the Representation on a Reference Set
paragraphs: Train preprocessing and the reconstruction model on suitable reference records. If training is dominated by faults, the model may learn to reproduce them. If it omits a normal operating mode, that mode may look unusual later.
Feature scales matter because squared error mixes coordinate contributions. Fit a scale on training records and retain it for validation and deployment.
interpretation: Our supplied arrays are already on comparable scales.

parts.title: 2. Keep Per-Feature Error Before Reducing
paragraphs: Subtract each reconstruction from its input and square each difference. A row mean gives one score per record, while the unreduced vector shows which features contributed.
parts.calculation:
Input = [1,3]; reconstruction = [1,1]
Squared errors = [0,4]
Row mean squared error = 2
interpretation: A different reduction or feature weighting changes the score and therefore its threshold.

parts.title: 3. Select the Alert Rule Separately
paragraphs: A model score is continuous. A threshold turns it into a decision. Choose the threshold using validation data and costs, then assess the final fixed rule on untouched records.
A reference percentile controls an empirical tail fraction in those records. It is not a universal guarantee of future false-alarm rate, particularly under drift.
interpretation: Use greater-than or greater-than-or-equal deliberately, including at the exact boundary.

examples.title: Inspect the mismatched features before raising an alert
paragraphs: The reconstruction gets the first feature right and misses the second. Square the feature errors before averaging them into one record score.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
record = np.array([2., 4.])
reconstructed = np.array([2., 2.])
squared_errors = (record - reconstructed) ** 2
print(squared_errors.tolist())
print(float(squared_errors.mean()))
interpretation: The single score hides which feature caused the error, so inspecting the contributions remains useful. Practice scores several records and applies a fixed alert threshold.

parts.title: 4. Investigate Failure Modes
paragraphs: A powerful model can learn an almost identity mapping and reconstruct anomalies too. A restrictive model can reject legitimate variation. Compare simple robust or density baselines and examine errors by operating mode.
When labels arrive late, store scores and model versions so later investigations can reconstruct why an alert occurred. Do not automatically treat every alert as a confirmed fault.
interpretation: The workshop returns an alert mask while preserving intermediate reconstruction errors for inspection.

practice.title: Can you score each reconstructed record?
practice.question: Can you score each reconstructed record?
task: Print row mean squared errors and alerts strictly above 1.5.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1.,3.],[2.,2.]])
rebuilt = np.array([[1.,1.],[2.,2.]])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1.,3.],[2.,2.]])
rebuilt = np.array([[1.,1.],[2.,2.]])
score = np.mean((x-rebuilt)**2,axis=1)
print(score.tolist())
print((score>1.5).tolist())
hints: Reduce feature columns, retaining a result per record.
The threshold applies after reduction.

practice.title: How many alerts were correct?
practice.question: How many alerts were correct?
task: Use threshold strictly above 2. Print true positives and false positives against supplied labels, where one means a confirmed fault.
practice.starter:

fault = np.array([0,1,0,0,1],dtype=bool)

The score exactly at two does not alert.

title: Recording Which Things Are Connected
blurb: A table of pump readings leaves out the pipes between pumps. A graph records those relationships so calculations can use the connections.
openingTitle: Could a Problem in One Pump Affect Another?
opening: Botie has a reading for each pump, but a pump’s behaviour can depend on what reaches it through the pipe network. Independent rows do not describe that network.
A graph adds two fundamental pieces: nodes for the things and edges for the relationships. We will turn a small network into an adjacency matrix and check exactly what each row means.

history.title: Using Relationships Alongside Measurements

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

blocks: Graph-based learning uses both measurements and the relationships between the things measured. Kipf and Welling’s graph-convolution work provides one influential example of using an adjacency structure to share information between nodes.
Before reaching a learned graph model, we need an unambiguous representation. Our pipe network is an invented example, and an edge records a connection rather than proving a causal effect.

quiz.prompt: Which node has two neighbours?
quiz.because: Row one contains two ones.

quiz.prompt: It must be deleted from the feature matrix.
quiz.because: Isolated nodes are still nodes.

given.data: A node has degree zero.

quiz.prompt: Which directed edge is recorded?
quiz.because: Follow the declared convention.

given.data: Rows are sources and columns are destinations. A[0,2]=1.

quiz.prompt: Its adjacency matrix is symmetric with a zero diagonal.
quiz.because: Each edge is represented in both directions.

given.data: An undirected unweighted graph has no self-loops.

build.title: Count the network’s connections
build.problem: Botie wants the degree of every pump in an undirected binary network.
build.challenge: Add the entries in each adjacency row.
build.why: Each row retains its node identity while its edge entries are counted.
build.limitation: For weighted graphs, row sums measure total weight instead of neighbour count.

intuition.title: Name the nodes
intuition.explanation: Keep one stable ordering.

intuition.title: Record edges
intuition.explanation: This first network is undirected.

intuition.title: Store neighbours by row
intuition.explanation: A one marks a connection to the column node.

intuition.title: A pump can exist without having a connection
intuition.explanation: The isolated pump still needs a row and a column. Its degree is zero, but deleting its row would remove the pump itself and shift the identities of the remaining entries.

scene.caption: An illustrative network with an isolated pump D.

parts.title: 1. Separate Node Features From Edges
paragraphs: A feature matrix stores readings with one row per node. An adjacency matrix stores relationships, with rows and columns using the same node order. The two matrices have different meanings even if both contain numbers.
An undirected connection appears in both directions. A directed edge needs an explicit convention; in this lesson a row identifies the source and a column the destination.
interpretation: Changing node order requires changing both adjacency axes and feature rows together.

parts.title: 2. Calculate Degree Without Guessing
paragraphs: For an unweighted graph without self-loops, row sums count outgoing neighbours. In an undirected graph they give degree. For weighted edges the same sum is total edge weight, which need not equal neighbour count.
interpretation: A node with no edges still exists and still needs a feature row.

parts.title: 3. Choose a Storage Structure
paragraphs: A dense adjacency matrix makes a small network easy to inspect but uses space for every possible pair. An edge list stores only existing edges as source-destination pairs. Sparse matrices support many of the same algebraic operations without storing every zero.
Duplicate entries require a policy. Counting the same physical pipe twice may accidentally double its influence when building a weighted matrix.
interpretation: The NumPy exercises use dense arrays for clarity, not as a recommendation for large networks.

examples.title: Read the neighbours of one pump from its row
paragraphs: This pump has a position for every possible neighbour, including itself. A one means an edge is present and the zero on its own position means no self-loop.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
pump_row = np.array([0, 1, 1, 1])
print(np.flatnonzero(pump_row).tolist())
print(int(pump_row.sum()))
interpretation: The neighbour indices identify three connections. Practice counts degrees across a complete adjacency matrix and checks the undirected symmetry.

parts.title: 4. Define What a Connection Permits
paragraphs: A physical pipe, a friendship, a citation, and a similarity edge imply different things. Decide whether messages may travel with or against a directed edge and whether edge weights express capacity, affinity, or another quantity.
A connection alone does not establish causation. Later learning can use relationships predictively even when their causal interpretation is unknown.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop first checks degrees before any information is passed through the network.

practice.title: Can you read the network’s degrees?
practice.question: Can you read the network’s degrees?

Symmetry compares both directions.

practice.title: Can you build an undirected matrix from edges?
practice.question: Can you build an undirected matrix from edges?
task: Create a four-node adjacency matrix from the unique edge list. Set both directions. Print degrees, including the isolated node.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
edges = np.array([[0,1],[1,2]])
n = 4
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
edges = np.array([[0,1],[1,2]])
n = 4
A = np.zeros((n,n),dtype=int)
for a,b in edges:
    A[a,b] = 1
    A[b,a] = 1
print(A.sum(axis=1).tolist())
hints: Allocate all four nodes before adding edges.
Do not invent a connection for node three.

reading.experimentIntro: Choose a pump row and count its neighbours. When changing an undirected connection, change the matching entry on the other side of the matrix as well.

reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Read Degrees and Build an Adjacency Matrix

title: Following Probability Through a Network
blurb: A random walker chooses among outgoing links. Follow the probability mass to see how graph structure changes where it accumulates.
openingTitle: Where Does a Walker Go From Here?
opening: Imagine Botie inspecting a network by choosing an outgoing connection at each step. A junction with several links gives several possible next positions.
We do not need to sample one route to describe every possibility. A probability vector and a transition matrix let us calculate where a whole collection of walkers would be expected to go.

history.title: Ranking Through Linked Structure

sources.title: Page and colleagues: The PageRank Citation Ranking

blocks: PageRank used a random-surfer interpretation to relate the importance of web pages to incoming links from other pages. Teleportation provides a way to leave a local link structure and makes the process less dependent on traps.

Our pipe-network walk first studies ordinary transitions. It is a structural probability calculation, not a physical fluid simulation; actual flow depends on pressures and capacities as well as connectivity.

quiz.prompt: Where is the mass after one step?
quiz.because: The first row sends it to node one.

quiz.prompt: Dividing its adjacency row by its degree is safe.
quiz.because: Its degree is zero; a policy is required.

given.data: A node has no outgoing edges.

quiz.prompt: Which calculation advances the distribution?
quiz.because: Destination mass sums source contributions.

given.data: Rows are current nodes. p is a row probability vector.

quiz.prompt: Its distribution can oscillate instead of converging.
quiz.because: The process has a period of two.

given.data: A two-node walk always switches to the other node.

build.title: Advance a probability distribution
build.problem: Botie has a row-stochastic transition matrix and current node probabilities.
build.challenge: Transpose the transition matrix, then multiply it by the current probability vector.
build.why: Each destination receives probability from all possible starting nodes.
build.limitation: The supplied matrix must already embody a declared dangling-node policy.

intuition.title: Begin at one node
intuition.explanation: The vector describes probabilities, not measured flow.

intuition.title: Choose among outgoing edges
intuition.explanation: The middle node of a three-node chain has two equally likely choices.

intuition.title: Advance the distribution
intuition.explanation: Probability spreads through allowed transitions.

parts.title: 1. Normalise Outgoing Weights
paragraphs: For non-negative adjacency weights, divide each row by its outgoing total to form transition probabilities. A positive weight is a relative choice weight, not a probability until normalised.
A node with no outgoing edges has a zero row. Choose a dangling-node policy explicitly. Our exercises make such a node stay at itself; PageRank often redistributes that probability instead.
interpretation: Every resulting transition row must sum to one.

parts.title: 2. Move Mass With the Correct Orientation
paragraphs: When rows are current nodes and columns next nodes, multiply a row probability vector by the transition matrix. Each destination collects contributions from all sources.
interpretation: Total probability remains one when the transition matrix is valid.

parts.title: 3. Recognise Cycles and Traps
paragraphs: An undirected two-node walk alternates forever rather than settling from every starting point. A disconnected component cannot reach another without an added transition. These are properties of the graph and process.
Teleportation mixes a link-following transition with a chosen restart distribution. It changes the process deliberately rather than fixing an arithmetic error.
interpretation: Do not assume every repeated matrix multiplication converges to one unique result.

examples.title: Collect arrivals from two possible starting nodes
paragraphs: Half the probability begins at each node. The first stays put; the second splits equally between staying and moving to the first.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
probability = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
transition = np.array([[1., 0.], [0.5, 0.5]])
contributions = probability[:, None] * transition
print(contributions.tolist())
print(contributions.sum(axis=0).tolist())
interpretation: Each row records one source node's contribution. Adding down the columns collects the probability arriving at each destination.

parts.title: 4. Use the Walk for the Right Question
paragraphs: Random walks can describe reachability patterns, ranking, or sampling of graph neighbourhoods. They do not automatically describe the actual movement of water, disease, or information.
Compare walk results under different edge definitions, and document the dangling-node and restart rules. Otherwise two implementations can disagree while each follows its own valid process.
interpretation: The workshop takes an already valid transition matrix so the movement of probability is visible.

P = np.array([[0.,1.,0.],[.5,0.,.5],[0.,1.,0.]])
for _ in range(2):
    p = p @ P
    print(p.tolist())

Use the result of one step as the input to the next.

Check both rows sum to one.

reading.experimentIntro: Start with probability concentrated at one node. Follow that node's outgoing row, then try a mixture of starting nodes and see their contributions combine at each destination.

title: Letting a Node Read Its Neighbours’ Measurements
blurb: A pump’s neighbours can provide useful context. Aggregate their readings while retaining the distinction between a node and its surroundings.
openingTitle: What Can the Nearby Pumps Tell Us?
opening: One pump reports low pressure. Its neighbours might reveal whether the whole region is affected or just that instrument. We need a calculation that gathers measurements from connected nodes.
Neighbour aggregation collects those values with a sum, mean, or another declared rule. It is the information-sharing step on which many graph models build.

history.title: Learning How to Combine Local Neighbourhoods

sources.title: Hamilton, Ying and Leskovec: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs

blocks: GraphSAGE learned functions for sampling and aggregating local neighbourhood information, allowing representations to be constructed from node features and neighbourhoods. This differs from storing a separate learned vector for every node identity.

Our lesson isolates a full-neighbour mean. It does not reproduce GraphSAGE’s sampling and learned combination, but makes the message-gathering operation visible before adding trainable transformations.

quiz.prompt: What is their mean?
quiz.because: Average the received values.

given.data: Middle node neighbours have readings [2,4].

quiz.prompt: The node’s own value belongs in its neighbour mean.
quiz.because: That would change the declared rule.

given.data: The aggregation excludes self.

quiz.prompt: What must the implementation specify?
quiz.because: No neighbour mean exists without a convention.

given.data: An isolated node has degree zero.

quiz.prompt: Distinct node features can become increasingly similar.
quiz.because: Repeated mixing can remove useful distinctions.

given.data: Repeated mean aggregation is applied many times.

build.title: Read neighbouring pumps
build.problem: Botie has an undirected adjacency matrix and aligned scalar readings.
build.challenge: Gather neighbouring readings with matrix multiplication, then divide each sum by its degree, returning zero for degree zero.
build.why: Each output remains attached to a node while summarising its neighbourhood.
build.limitation: The zero fallback is explicit. For directed graphs, choose message orientation before multiplying.

intuition.title: Start with one feature per node
intuition.explanation: The graph is a three-node chain.

intuition.title: Collect adjacent readings
intuition.explanation: The middle node sees both ends.

intuition.title: Average without changing row identity
intuition.explanation: Return one neighbour summary per node.

parts.title: 1. Define Which Nodes Send Messages
paragraphs: In our undirected graph, a node receives from every adjacent node. Multiplying adjacency by a feature vector sums neighbouring values. For directed graphs, row orientation must match the intended message direction.
A message may later include edge features or a learned transform. Begin with raw scalar readings so you can check which values reached each node.
interpretation: Node feature order and adjacency order must match exactly.

parts.title: 2. Choose Sum or Mean Deliberately
paragraphs: A sum changes with both neighbour values and neighbour count. A mean removes that direct degree scaling. Neither is universally better: total load and typical neighbouring pressure are different questions.
parts.calculation:
Readings = [2,8,4]
Neighbour sums = [8,6,8]
Degrees = [1,2,1]
Neighbour means = [8,3,8]
interpretation: An isolated node has no neighbour mean; our implementation returns zero with that policy stated.

parts.title: 3. Keep Own and Neighbour Features Distinct
paragraphs: The node’s own measurement may remain valuable even when neighbours disagree. A learned model can concatenate own features with the aggregate or add a separately transformed self contribution.
Adding self-loops before averaging is another rule, but it changes the denominator and the meaning of the summary. Do not silently substitute one for another.
interpretation: This lesson excludes self from the neighbour mean. The next lesson introduces self-loops explicitly.

examples.title: Average the readings attached to one node's neighbours
paragraphs: The adjacency row selects two neighbours from the same ordered reading array. Keep their identities during selection before reducing their readings to one average.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
adjacency_row = np.array([0, 1, 1])
readings = np.array([20., 4., 10.])
neighbour_readings = readings[adjacency_row.astype(bool)]
print(neighbour_readings.tolist())
print(float(neighbour_readings.mean()))
interpretation: The node's own reading of twenty is excluded by this row. Practice computes all nodes' summaries and handles the case where no neighbour is selected.

parts.title: 4. Avoid Washing Out Differences
paragraphs: Repeated averaging spreads information farther across the graph. It can also make different nodes’ representations increasingly similar, reducing the distinctions needed for prediction.
Useful context depends on the edge definition. Connected nodes do not always share labels or operating modes. Evaluate whether the chosen aggregation helps the actual task.
interpretation: The workshop returns neighbour context, not a trained node classifier.

practice.title: Can you collect neighbour means?
practice.question: Can you collect neighbour means?
task: For the three-node chain, print neighbour sums and means.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0.,1.,0.],[1.,0.,1.],[0.,1.,0.]])
x = np.array([2.,8.,4.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0.,1.,0.],[1.,0.,1.],[0.,1.,0.]])
x = np.array([2.,8.,4.])
total = A @ x
degree = A.sum(axis=1)
print(total.tolist())
print((total/degree).tolist())
hints: Matrix multiplication gathers each row’s connected values.
Divide by degree after gathering.

practice.title: Can you preserve an isolated node without dividing by zero?
practice.question: Can you preserve an isolated node without dividing by zero?
task: Compute neighbour means, returning zero for nodes with no neighbours. Print the result.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0.,1.,0.],[1.,0.,0.],[0.,0.,0.]])
x = np.array([3.,7.,9.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0.,1.,0.],[1.,0.,0.],[0.,0.,0.]])
x = np.array([3.,7.,9.])
degree = A.sum(axis=1)
means = np.divide(A @ x,degree,out=np.zeros(3),where=degree>0)
print(means.tolist())
hints: Use np.divide with an output and a where mask.
Zero is the chosen empty-neighbour convention.

reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Calculate Neighbour Means and Handle Isolation
